analysis.one_liner: Declares a national housing emergency and uses wartime production powers to spur homebuilding and loosen zoning rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in January 2026 by Senator Elissa Slotkin with zero cosponsors; read twice and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the President to declare a national housing emergency and use the Defense Production Act — a wartime law for ramping up critical production — to expand the supply of construction materials and support residential building [S2]. While the emergency is in effect, it would suspend a set of federal rules that slow HUD-funded housing projects, including some environmental reviews, and would bar state and local governments from enforcing land-use rules that substantially burden homebuilding [S2]. It would also condition federal block grants, like transportation funding, on states and cities showing positive housing growth and taking steps to allow denser housing [S2]. The emergency would end when 4 million additional units are built or on October 1, 2031, whichever comes first [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Renters and prospective homebuyers, who the bill's findings say face a shortage of at least 4 million housing units and a market where about 75 percent of households cannot afford a median-priced home [S2]. Construction workers and building-materials producers would also gain as production ramps up [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Adds residential construction and rehabilitation to the Defense Production Act, allowing the President to prioritize and incentivize domestic production of materials needed to build and rehabilitate housing [S2].

During the emergency, it strips federal rules that slow housing projects, including certain environmental reviews for HUD-funded preservation and infill projects, and requires a single environmental review when multiple federal programs fund one project [S2].

It bars states and localities from imposing land-use regulations that substantially burden housing construction, and it ties federal block grants to a 'Pro-Growth Requirement' demanding positive housing growth and steps like allowing duplexes and accessory dwelling units, cutting parking minimums, and speeding permits [S2].

The bill's findings cite a shortage of at least 4 million units, a first-time homebuyer share at a record low of 21 percent, and a projected 10 million-unit deficit by 2035, and estimate closing the gap could add nearly 2 million jobs and about $2 trillion to GDP through 2035 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments lose significant control over land use, since the bill preempts local zoning decisions that burden housing and conditions federal grants on demonstrating housing growth [S2]. Communities near federally funded housing would face reduced environmental review, and the bill pushes federal rules (like Buy America waivers) out the door on a 30-day clock or they are deemed approved [S2].

drawbacks.text: Suspending federal environmental review requirements for HUD-funded housing projects during the emergency removes a layer of scrutiny that protects communities from poorly sited or environmentally harmful development [S2].

The prohibition on local land-use rules that 'substantially burden' housing construction is a broad federal preemption of zoning decisions traditionally made by cities and counties, raising federalism and local-control concerns [S2].

Conditioning federal block grants — including transportation funding — on demonstrating positive housing growth each year could squeeze communities where population and demand are flat or falling [S2].

The bill sets the 2009 International Residential Code as its minimum standard during the emergency, which is a notably older code than current editions, so the quality and energy-efficiency floor for emergency-era construction is modest [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are high and real: housing is the largest expense for most households, and the bill attacks supply, the root of the affordability problem, with production incentives, deregulation, and pressure on local zoning. The trade-offs are concentrated in the deregulation half — waived environmental reviews, a 15-year-old building code floor, and sweeping preemption of local land use — which shift risk onto the communities hosting new construction. Whether the bill is a good bargain depends heavily on how the emergency is run; the text leaves much to federal agencies.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Slotkin introduced it on January 8, 2026, the Senate read it twice and sent it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, and the committee has not scheduled any further action on it [S4].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on January 8, 2026 [S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S4].
The only actions in the bill's history are introduction and the committee referral; there has been no markup, vote, or movement since [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, no one has moved: the bill sits untouched, which leaves the housing-supply status quo in place — a situation that benefits incumbent local governments holding zoning power and existing property owners whose home values the shortage inflates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo — local zoning power and rising home values

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote record to judge; the bill's sole sponsor is a Democrat and it has attracted zero cosponsors from either party [S3].

industries.note: The bill expands Defense Production Act authority to housing materials, suspends rules that slow projects, and pushes localities to permit more building, directly increasing construction work — the bill's findings estimate over 700,000 construction jobs [S2]. More building is exactly what affordability advocates want, so builders' interests run alongside the public's here [S2].

Adding residential construction to the Defense Production Act would direct federal incentives toward domestic production of housing materials [S2]. Faster, cheaper material supply supports the same affordability goal the public wants.

The bill preempts local land-use regulations that substantially burden housing and conditions federal block grants on demonstrating positive housing growth each year [S2]. Local zoning authority and the leverage it gives existing neighborhoods is what this bill takes aim at.

A large increase in housing supply would moderate rents and slow the home-price appreciation that existing owners benefit from [S2]. Their financial interest runs against the affordability gains renters and buyers would get.

HUD-funded housing would be exempt from federal environmental review during the emergency, and Buy America waivers would be deemed approved if not processed within 30 days [S2]. Groups and agencies that rely on review processes to safeguard communities lose that check.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action months after referral, and a sponsor from the minority party, the bill's realistic path is to sit in the Senate Banking Committee until the 119th Congress ends, unless housing becomes a vehicle issue in a larger package. Single-sponsor housing bills at this stage almost never reach the floor on their own.
